entries.question: What is cement?
entries.answer: Cement's a fine powder that binds sand, gravel, and water together — it's the glue that holds concrete and mortar in place. Without it, you've just got a pile of aggregate going nowhere.

entries.question: What is the difference between cement and concrete?
entries.answer: Cement is an ingredient — concrete is the finished product you make with it. Mix your cement with sand, aggregate, and water and you've got concrete; the cement alone won't do the job.

entries.question: What is cement used for?
entries.answer: You'll find cement at the heart of almost every build — foundations, driveways, walls, screeds, mortar for brickwork, and general concrete work. If it's structural and it sets hard, cement's almost certainly involved.

entries.question: How much does a 25kg bag of cement cover?
entries.answer: A 25kg bag gives you roughly 0.012m³ of concrete, though that'll shift depending on your mix ratio. It's worth calculating your volume first so you're not short on site.

entries.question: How many bags of cement are on a pallet?
entries.answer: A standard UK pallet holds 56 bags of 25kg cement — that's 1,400kg in total, so make sure your access and ground conditions can take the weight before delivery.

entries.question: How much does a bag of cement weigh?
entries.answer: The standard UK bag weighs 25kg — manageable enough for one person, but you'll want to mind your back if you're shifting a full pallet's worth.

entries.question: How long does cement last?
entries.answer: Stored dry and unopened, cement'll typically last around 3 months — but don't push it if you can help it. Use it as soon as you can and you'll get the best strength out of it.

entries.question: Can cement go out of date?
entries.answer: It absolutely can — old cement draws in moisture from the air and starts to pre-hydrate, which means it loses strength before it's even mixed. If your bags feel lumpy or have gone hard in places, don't risk it.

entries.question: Is cement waterproof?
entries.answer: Standard cement isn't waterproof on its own — you'll need to add a waterproofing admixture if you want real resistance to moisture. It's a common assumption that catches people out, so worth knowing upfront.

entries.question: How long does cement take to set?
entries.answer: You'll see initial set kick in within 30–60 minutes, so don't dawdle once it's mixed. Full curing takes around 28 days — that's when it reaches its rated strength, not when it just feels solid.

entries.question: What is rapid-set cement?
entries.answer: Rapid-set cement hardens far quicker than standard — ideal when you need a repair done and can't wait around for a normal cure. It's a favourite on site when downtime costs money.

entries.question: Can I use cement by itself?
entries.answer: Don't use cement neat — it'll shrink and crack as it cures. You always want to mix it with sand or aggregate to give it body and keep it stable.

entries.question: What is mortar?
entries.answer: Mortar is what you get when you mix cement with sand and water — it's the stuff that holds your bricks and blocks together. Bricklayers'll tell you the mix ratio matters a lot depending on what you're building.

entries.question: What is concrete?
entries.answer: Concrete is cement combined with sand, aggregate, and water — once it cures, you've got one of the most durable building materials around. Get your mix ratio right and it'll last decades.

entries.question: What is screed?
entries.answer: Screed is a cement-based mix you lay over a structural floor to create a smooth, level surface ready for your final finish. Flooring trades rely on it constantly — get the consistency wrong and nothing sits flat.

entries.question: Can cement be painted?
entries.answer: Yes — but you'll want to let it fully cure first, otherwise the paint won't bond properly and you'll end up peeling it off again within months. Give it the full curing time, prep the surface well, and you'll get a finish that actually lasts.

entries.question: How should cement be stored?
entries.answer: Keep your bags dry, sealed, and raised off the ground — even a damp floor will start pulling moisture into the bag and ruin the cement before you've opened it. A pallet and a decent sheet of polythene go a long way on site.

entries.question: Does cement expire?
entries.answer: It does — moisture is the enemy, and once it gets into the bag it starts a slow reaction that kills the strength before you've even mixed a thing. If your bags feel lumpy or have gone hard in patches, don't risk it on anything structural.

entries.question: Can wet cement be reused?
entries.answer: No — once cement starts setting, that's it, you can't remix it back to life. Only mix what you can realistically use in one go, and you'll save yourself a lot of waste.

entries.question: Is cement environmentally friendly?
entries.answer: Cement production does generate significant carbon emissions — it's one of the industry's bigger environmental challenges. That said, lower-carbon alternatives are becoming more widely available, so it's worth asking your merchant what options they stock if that matters to your project.

entries.question: Which cement is best for foundations?
entries.answer: For most domestic foundations, General Purpose Cement does the job well — it's the workhorse of the range and what most builders reach for first. If you're dealing with sulphate-rich ground or aggressive soil conditions, have a word with your merchant about a more specialist mix.

entries.question: Can cement be used in cold weather?
entries.answer: You can use it in cold weather, but below around 5°C the curing process slows right down — and if it freezes before it's set, you'll end up with weak, damaged concrete. Protect fresh pours with insulating blankets and keep an eye on overnight temperatures.

entries.question: Can cement be used in hot weather?
entries.answer: Hot weather speeds up drying, which sounds handy but actually increases the risk of cracking if the surface dries out too fast. Keep your mix shaded where you can, dampen the substrate beforehand, and consider curing with a damp hessian cover in really warm conditions.

entries.question: How much water should I add?
entries.answer: Always follow the manufacturer's instructions on the bag — water ratios matter more than most people realise. A mix that's too wet might be easier to work with, but it'll come out weaker and more prone to cracking once it's set.

entries.question: What colour is cement?
entries.answer: Most cement is grey — that familiar blue-grey you'll see on every building site. White cement is also available if you need a cleaner base for decorative work or coloured finishes.

entries.question: What is white cement?
entries.answer: White cement is made with purer raw materials to give you a bright, clean finish — it's the go-to for decorative renders, architectural concrete, and coloured mixes where grey would muddy the final colour. It tends to be more expensive than standard grey, but for the right job it's worth it.

entries.question: Can cement be coloured?
entries.answer: Yes — you add specialist pigments to the mix to get the colour you're after. White cement gives you the truest, most vivid results if colour accuracy matters, since grey cement will shift the final tone.

entries.question: Is cement dangerous?
entries.answer: Wet cement is alkaline and can cause serious skin irritation and chemical burns — don't underestimate it, even on short jobs. Always wear gloves and eye protection, and if it gets on your skin, rinse it off thoroughly with clean water straight away.

entries.question: Can cement be recycled?
entries.answer: Concrete made from cement can often be crushed down and reused as aggregate — it's a common practice on demolition sites and a decent way to keep material out of landfill. The recycled aggregate won't replace virgin material in every application, but it's useful for hardcore and sub-base work.

entries.question: How long before walking on fresh concrete?
entries.answer: You're typically looking at 24–48 hours before light foot traffic — but that's in reasonable conditions, so factor in temperature and humidity on the day. Don't push it too early; surface damage at this stage is a pain to put right.

entries.question: How long before driving on concrete?
entries.answer: Wait 7 days before light vehicles and 28 days before you park anything heavy. Drive too soon and you'll crack it.

entries.question: Does rain damage fresh cement?
entries.answer: Yes — heavy rain washes cement out of the mix and weakens the surface. Cover fresh pours with polythene until the initial set holds.

entries.question: What is General Purpose Cement?
entries.answer: General Purpose (CEM II 32.5N) is the standard cement most merchants stock — good for domestic foundations, mortar, concrete and everyday work.

entries.question: What is Sulphate Resistant Cement?
entries.answer: SRC's for ground with high sulphate content — clay soils, some brownfield sites. Standard cement breaks down in sulphates; SRC doesn't. Ask a groundworker if you're not sure whether you need it.

entries.question: What is Masonry Cement?
entries.answer: Masonry cement's blended for bricklaying and rendering — more workable than General Purpose, holds moisture better while you're laying bricks.

entries.question: Can cement crack?
entries.answer: Yes — mainly from drying too fast, poor mix ratio, or moving ground underneath. Cure properly and mix right, most cracks are avoidable.

entries.question: Why does concrete crack?
entries.answer: Shrinkage as it dries, movement in the ground, curing too fast, or too much water in the mix. Hairline cracks are normal. Bigger cracks mean something's moving.

entries.question: Can cracked concrete be repaired?
entries.answer: Small cracks fill with concrete repair mortar or a flexible sealant. Bigger cracks in structural work, get a builder's eye on them first.

entries.question: How strong is concrete?
entries.answer: Domestic concrete typically runs 20–40 MPa. Foundations at the lower end, structural work higher. Ready-mix suppliers can spec exactly what you need.

entries.question: What is the strongest cement?
entries.answer: For strongest concrete, use CEM I 52.5N with a low water-cement ratio (0.4 or less). Most domestic work is fine with CEM II 32.5N — go higher-spec only when the design calls for it.
entries.fact_check_flag: Original dodged the question — gave a specific answer while noting most jobs don't need it.

entries.question: How many bags make one cubic metre of concrete?
entries.answer: About 13–14 bags of 25kg cement per m³ in a standard 1:2:4 mix — roughly 350kg cement per m³.

entries.question: Can I lay concrete myself?
entries.answer: For small pours — fence posts, a shed base, a small path — yes. Bigger slabs and structural work, get a groundworker in. Ready-mix delivery is worth every penny once you're past 1m³.

entries.question: Why is curing important?
entries.answer: Curing's what actually gives concrete its strength. Keep it damp for the first 3–7 days — mist it, cover with hessian, use a curing compound. Skip curing and you lose up to 30% of the strength.

entries.question: Should I wet concrete while curing?
entries.answer: Yes — misting the surface for the first week or covering with damp hessian and polythene keeps the chemical reaction going properly. Dry too fast, it cracks.

entries.question: What happens if too much water is added?
entries.answer: Too much water weakens the mix badly — you end up with a chalky, dusty surface and poor strength. Stick to the manufacturer's ratio.

entries.question: Can frozen cement be used?
entries.answer: No. Cement that has frozen or become damp should not be used.
